memoryText: For the eyes of the LORD run to and fro throughout the whole earth, to give strong support to those whose heart is blameless toward him.
readingInstruction: No new reading today. Read 2 Chronicles 16:9 slowly, several times, and then say it from memory. Read the meditation and the week in review, and choose one of the three questions to write about, pray over, or share with someone.
memoryVerseMeditation:
This verse was spoken as a rebuke to King Asa, but it is full of encouragement. It was meant to say, “You could have had so much more help if you had trusted me.” For us, it is an invitation.

“For the eyes of the LORD run to and fro.” The image is of God’s active attention. His eyes are not still. They run, like a scout surveying the land. The LORD is looking, searching, always watching. Nothing is hidden from him. For those who want to hide, this is a threat. For those who are seeking him, it is a comfort.

“Throughout the whole earth.” His watch covers the entire world, not just Israel. No place is outside his sight. No believer is forgotten, however remote.

“To give strong support.” This is what he is looking for: someone to help. The word means to strengthen or make firm. He is not scanning in order to catch people out but to find those he can support. God is looking for people to help.

“To those whose heart is blameless toward him.” The condition is a heart that is whole, undivided, and loyal. “Blameless” does not mean sinless. Asa was no angel, and neither was David. It means a heart that is fully turned toward him, that does not divide its trust. God looks for those whose reliance is wholly on him.

When you feel alone, small, or unnoticed, remember that God’s eyes are running through the whole earth with a purpose: to help you. Give him a heart that is completely his.
weekInReview: This week you followed the kings of Judah through the Chronicler’s eyes. You saw Solomon’s glory fade into Rehoboam’s folly, and the kingdom divide. You watched Asa cry out to the LORD against a million Ethiopians and then rely on Syria and doctors in his old age. You saw Jehoshaphat teach the law, make an unwise alliance, and then lead the nation in prayer: “We do not know what to do, but our eyes are on you.” You followed the tragedy of Athaliah and the rescue of baby Joash, then Joash’s fall after Jehoiada’s death. You read of Uzziah’s pride and Jotham’s steady faithfulness, and Hezekiah’s reform and Passover. The Chronicler’s lesson is clear: seek the LORD and you will find him; forsake him and he will forsake you.
reflectionQuestions: The Chronicler repeats the word “seek” again and again. What does seeking the LORD look like in your daily rhythm?
Asa began well and ended poorly. What practices might help you to finish well?
Hezekiah prayed, “May the good LORD pardon everyone who sets his heart to seek God.” How does the gospel assure us of that pardon?
prayerPrompts: Ask God for a heart that is wholly his.
Thank him that his eyes run to and fro to strengthen the blameless.
